title: The Red Ball
summary: Max the dog loses his favorite ball in the park. Can he find it again?
teachingMethodReason: Meets the course's own criteria for story-based instruction: a formulaic opening ("This is Max..."), a clear problem (the ball is lost) through a search to a resolution, and patterned, repetitive sentence structure. It doesn't meet TBL (the reader never does a task - Willis 1996/Nunan 2006) or CLIL (no other-subject content - Coyle et al. 2010); it's the narrative craft itself, not an add-on task, that earns this label.
grammarFeatures: Simple present tense, used to narrate the story
"To be" statements (Max is a dog, Max is happy)
introFunFacts: 🎉 Get ready! Watch for the tiny word 'IS' - it tells us what something IS like. Max IS happy! The ball IS red!
🕵️ 'Where' is a detective word! We use it to ask about places, like 'Where is the ball?'
🎨 Can you spot the color word hiding in this story?

quiz.question: What kind of animal is Max?
What color is Max's ball?
Where does Max lose his ball?
How does Max feel when he finds the ball?

pages.text: This is Max. Max is a {{dog}}. Max is {{happy}}.

vocab.definition: An animal that says woof and likes to play.
Feeling good, and smiling.

pages.text: Max has a {{ball}}. The ball is {{red}}. Max likes the ball.

vocab.definition: A round toy that you can throw, kick, or bounce.
A bright color, like an apple or a strawberry.

pages.text: Max runs in the {{park}}. He drops the ball. Where is the ball?

vocab.definition: A green place outside with grass and trees, where you can play.

pages.text: Max looks under a {{tree}}. He looks near the {{bench}}. No ball!

vocab.definition: A tall plant with a trunk, branches, and leaves.
A long seat for sitting outside.

pages.text: Max finds the ball next to a {{flower}}. Max is happy again! Woof, woof!

vocab.definition: A pretty plant that can smell nice and comes in many colors.

title: My Family
summary: Meet a happy family and learn simple words for the people you love.
teachingMethodReason: A themed vocabulary description (family members, home) with no problem-to-resolution arc or sequence of events, so it doesn't meet the course's story-based criteria the way a real narrative does. It's thematically coherent (family), but theme-based instruction requires several different linked activities around a topic, not a single reading text - and there's no task (not TBL) or subject content (not CLIL) either. So it's General: solid vocabulary input, not yet built around a specific named methodology.
introFunFacts: 👪 Big secret: the word 'MY' means something belongs to YOU! My family, my book, my home!
💛 Watch for 'likes to' - it tells us what someone loves doing, like 'she likes to read'.
🔍 Can you find all the family members hiding in this story?

quiz.question: What does the mother like to do?
Who works at a table?
What pet does the sister have?
Where is the family happy?

pages.text: This is my {{family}}. We live in a small {{house}}.

vocab.definition: The people you live with, like your parents and siblings.
A building where people live.

pages.text: This is my {{mother}}. She likes to read a {{book}}.

vocab.definition: Your mom, a parent.
Pages with words and pictures that you read.

pages.text: This is my {{father}}. He works at a {{table}}.

vocab.definition: Your dad, a parent.
A piece of furniture you eat or work on.

pages.text: This is my {{sister}}. She has a {{cat}}.

vocab.definition: A girl who has the same parents as you.
A small furry pet that says meow.

pages.text: I love my family. We are happy at {{home}}.

vocab.definition: The place where you live with your family.

title: A Day at the Park
summary: Mia and Tom spend a sunny day playing, exploring, and making a new furry friend.
teachingMethodReason: Has real story structure - temporal sequence ("First... Then... Before they went home..."), a mini problem (the ball flies over the fence) resolved through action, and a formulaic closing ("It was a wonderful day") - meeting the course's story-based criteria. Still not TBL (the reader doesn't do the problem-solving - Willis 1996) or CLIL (no other-subject content). Note: the lost-ball beat is structurally close to a real TBL task - a prompt asking the reader to guess where the ball landed before the reveal would upgrade this to genuine TBL.
grammarFeatures: Simple past tense (went, played, kicked, sat)
Infinitive of purpose (climbed... to find the ball)
introFunFacts: ⏪ This story already happened! Watch for words like 'went', 'played' and 'sat' - that's how we talk about the past.
1️⃣ Look for 'First', 'Then' and 'Before' - these little words put the story in order.
🎯 'Mia climbed over the fence TO FIND the ball' - the word 'to' tells us WHY she did it!

quiz.question: Where did Mia and Tom go?
What happened to the ball?
What did the little dog want?
What did they do before going home?

pages.text: Yesterday, Mia and Tom went to the park. It was a sunny day, so they were very {{excited}}.

vocab.definition: Feeling very happy and full of energy about something.

pages.text: First, they played with a red ball under a big tree. Tom kicked the ball, and it flew over the {{fence}}!

vocab.definition: A wall made of wood or metal around a garden or field.

pages.text: Mia {{climbed}} over the fence to find the ball. She found it next to some yellow flowers.

vocab.definition: Went up or over something using your hands and feet.

pages.text: Then, they sat on a bench and ate their lunch. They had {{sandwiches}} and juice.

vocab.definition: Food made of bread with something tasty inside.
A meal you eat in the middle of the day.

pages.text: A little dog came near them. It wanted a {{piece}} of their sandwich! Mia gave it a small piece.

vocab.definition: A small part of something.

pages.text: Before they went home, Mia and Tom watched the clouds and talked about their {{favorite}} animals. It was a {{wonderful}} day.

vocab.definition: The one you like best.
Very good; amazing.

title: The Mystery of the Missing Cat
summary: When Anna's cat vanishes, she and her friend Ben follow the clues to solve the mystery.
teachingMethodReason: The clearest story-based example in the library: formulaic opening, introduction of the problem (the cat vanishes), a series of events building suspense (searching, clues, following the trail), and a resolution with a moral-ish close (relieved, mystery solved) - exactly the discourse pattern the course's story-based instruction deck describes. It's not yet TBL: the characters solve a problem, but the reader doesn't - per Willis (1996)/Nunan (2006), TBL requires the learner to use language to reach a real outcome themselves (e.g. listing clues, predicting the cat's location). It's the strongest candidate in the library to convert to genuine TBL: add a task like 'Where do you think Whiskers is? List two places to check' before the page 5 reveal, and it would qualify.
grammarFeatures: Verb + infinitive / gerund complements (decided to investigate, started looking)
Simple passive voice (the mystery was solved)
Present participle clauses (looking a little embarrassed)
introFunFacts: 🕵️ You're a detective today! Watch for 'clues' - small things that help solve a mystery.
❓ 'Maybe Whiskers went this way' - 'maybe' means we're not sure yet. Detectives guess before they know!
🔎 Look for 'decided to' and 'started looking' - two verbs teaming up to say what someone did next.

quiz.question: What went missing at the start of the story?
What clue did Anna find near the fence?
Who joined Anna in the search?
Where was Whiskers all along?

pages.text: Anna's cat, Whiskers, {{disappeared}} on Monday morning. She {{searched}} the house but couldn't find him anywhere.

vocab.definition: Suddenly could not be seen; went missing.
Looked carefully for something.

pages.text: Anna decided to {{investigate}}. She grabbed a magnifying glass and started looking for {{clues}} in the garden.

vocab.definition: To try to find out the truth about something.
Small pieces of information that help solve a mystery.

pages.text: She {{noticed}} some paw prints near the fence. Maybe Whiskers went into the {{neighbor's}} yard this way.

vocab.definition: Saw or became aware of something.
Belonging to the person who lives next door.

pages.text: Anna's friend Ben {{joined}} the search. Together, they {{followed}} the paw prints all the way to an old tree.

vocab.definition: Came together with someone to do something.
Went after or behind something.

pages.text: {{Suddenly}}, they heard a soft meow coming from above. Whiskers was stuck in the tree, looking a little {{embarrassed}}!

vocab.definition: Happening quickly and without warning.
Feeling shy or awkward about something.

pages.text: Ben climbed up {{carefully}} and brought Whiskers down. Anna hugged her cat tightly, {{relieved}} that the mystery was finally {{solved}}.

vocab.definition: Doing something with a lot of attention, to avoid mistakes.
Feeling calm again after being worried.
Found the answer to a problem.

title: Ruby's Picnic Basket
summary: Ruby the rabbit wants a picnic. Can you help her pack the basket?
teachingMethodReason: This book has a real task, not just a story about one. On page 4 the reader must tap and build their own list of picnic items before the story reveals what Ruby actually packs - meeting Willis (1996/2006)'s 'Listing' task type (brainstorming/fact-finding toward a completed list) and Nunan (2006)'s bar for a task: the outcome is still unknown, meaning is primary, and there's a real goal to complete. The resolution page then lets the reader compare their own list to Ruby's, which is the 'report' stage of Willis's pre-task -> task cycle -> language focus structure.
introFunFacts: 🧺 Big job today: help build a LIST! Ruby needs YOUR help finding picnic food.
❓ Watch for 'What DOES she need?' - we add 'does' when we ask about one person (he/she/it)!
👉 Look for action words like 'Tap' and 'Help' - they tell YOU what to do!

quiz.question: What is Ruby packing for?
What color is the apple Ruby finds?
Where does Ruby eat her picnic?
What does Ruby NOT need for her picnic?

pages.text: Ruby wants to have a {{picnic}} today! She looks at her empty {{basket}}. What does she need?

vocab.definition: A meal you eat outside, like in a park or garden.
A container you can use to carry food.

vocab.definition: Food made of bread with something tasty inside.
A round, crunchy fruit.
A small container you drink from.

title: Leo Grows a Sunflower
summary: Leo plants a tiny seed. Can you put the steps in the right order to grow a sunflower?
teachingMethodReason: A genuine task, not a quiz: on page 2 the reader must reason out the correct order of four gardening steps (using world knowledge - a seed must be planted before it sprouts) before the story confirms the real sequence. This meets Willis (1996/2006)'s 'Ordering and sorting' task type (sequencing toward a set of information ordered by a real criterion) and Nunan (2006)'s bar for a task: the outcome is still unknown, meaning is primary, and there's a real goal. The following page's position-by-position comparison is the 'report' stage of Willis's pre-task -> task cycle -> language focus structure.
introFunFacts: 🌱 Big job in this book: YOU put the steps in the right order before the story shows you!
🔢 Watch for 'First', 'Then', 'After' and 'Finally' - they are the order things happened.
💭 'Leo WANTED TO GROW a sunflower' - 'wanted to' tells us what someone hoped to do.

quiz.question: What did Leo want to grow?
What did Leo have besides a tiny seed?
How often did Leo water it?
How did Leo feel at the end?

pages.text: Last spring, Leo wanted to grow a beautiful {{sunflower}}. He had a tiny {{seed}} and some {{soil}}.

vocab.definition: A tall flower with a big yellow head.
A tiny thing that grows into a plant.
The dark earth that plants grow in.

pages.text: These four things happened when Leo grew his sunflower. Tap them in the order they happened!
First, Leo planted the {{seed}} in the soil.

vocab.definition: A tiny thing that grows into a plant.

pages.text: Then, he watered it every day.
After a few days, a tiny {{sprout}} appeared!

vocab.definition: A small new plant just starting to grow.

pages.text: Finally, a big {{sunflower}} bloomed! Leo was very {{proud}}.

vocab.definition: A tall flower with a big yellow head.
Feeling very happy about something you did.

title: Ben's Missing Backpack
summary: Ben can't find his backpack before school. Where do you think it is?
teachingMethodReason: A genuine problem-solving task: on page 4 the reader must weigh the clues (the backpack isn't where it always is; his little sister was playing all morning) and choose ONE most-likely location before the story reveals the truth. This meets Willis (1996/2006)'s 'Problem solving' task type (analyzing, reasoning, decision making -> problems solved and evaluated) - unlike a story where a character solves a problem for the reader, here the reader makes the actual decision under real uncertainty (several plausible locations, only one is right). The following page's report stage reveals the answer and how the reader's guess compares, gently regardless of outcome.
grammarFeatures: Making predictions and guesses (Where do you think...?)
introFunFacts: 🎒 Your turn to be the detective: YOU decide where the backpack is before the story tells you.
🔀 Watch for the word 'but' - it warns you something surprising is coming next.
💬 See the "quotation marks"? They show the exact words someone said out loud.

quiz.question: Where does Ben always keep his backpack?
How did Ben feel when he couldn't find it?
Where was the backpack really?
Did Ben catch the bus?

pages.text: Ben was getting ready for school, but he {{couldn't}} find his {{backpack}} anywhere. He felt {{worried}}.

vocab.definition: Was not able to.
A bag you carry on your back, for school.
Feeling nervous that something is wrong.

pages.text: He always keeps it by the front door, but it wasn't there today.
His little {{sister}} played in her room all morning. She likes to play with his things.

vocab.definition: A girl who has the same parents as you.

pages.text: Ben can't find his backpack! Where do you think it is? Pick the place you think is most likely.

title: Zoe and the Animal Homes
summary: Zoe explores where different animals live and why. Learn about animal homes around the world!
teachingMethodReason: Meets Coyle, Hood & Marsh (2010)'s 4 C's Framework, unlike the library's other books which only teach language: Content - real science/geography knowledge (which habitat each animal lives in and why), not just animal-name vocabulary; Communication - the target language (habitat, ocean, desert, forest, live in) is the vehicle for learning that content, not the end in itself; Cognition - the book asks the reader to connect an animal to its habitat, a real categorization skill, not just recall; Culture - the closing page ('Animals live in many different homes around the world') is an intercultural/global-awareness statement, not just a story ending. This is expository, not narrative - there's no problem-to-resolution arc, so it doesn't read as Story-based; the content-language balance is what earns CLIL here.
grammarFeatures: Prepositional phrases of place (in the water, in the sky)
introFunFacts: 🌍 Today's mission: learn about ANIMAL HOMES around the world - that's called a 'habitat'!
📍 Watch for little location words like 'in the ocean' or 'in the sky' - they tell us WHERE something is!
🐫 Fun fact: some homes are hot and dry, some are wet and cold. Can you guess which animal lives where?

quiz.question: Where do fish live?
Where do camels live?
Where do birds live?

quiz.question: Where do bears live?

pages.text: Zoe loves animals! Today, she wants to learn about their {{homes}}. Every animal has a special {{habitat}}.

vocab.definition: The places where people or animals live.
The natural place where an animal lives.

title: Sam and the Four Seasons
summary: Sam watches the big tree outside the window change all year long. Discover why the seasons change!
teachingMethodReason: Meets Coyle, Hood & Marsh (2010)'s 4 C's Framework: Content - real science knowledge about seasonal change (temperature, plant growth/loss) rather than just season-name vocabulary; Communication - present-tense factual language and cause ('because') are the vehicle for that content; Cognition - the book asks the reader to connect a cause (temperature, sunlight) to an effect (leaves growing or falling), not just recall a season's name; Culture - the closing page ('the seasons are different in different parts of the world') is a light intercultural/global-awareness note. Deliberately written in the simple present for general truths rather than past-tense narrative, unlike this level's other books (a-day-at-the-park, leo-grows-a-sunflower), so the library covers a wider range of A2 grammar rather than repeating the same past-tense/sequencing pattern.
grammarFeatures: Simple present tense for general facts/truths
Prepositions of time (in spring, in summer)
introFunFacts: 🌍 This book tells you things that are ALWAYS true, so it says 'grow' and 'falls' - not 'grew' and 'fell'.
🤔 Watch for the word 'because' - it always tells you WHY something happens!
🌡️ 'Warmer' and 'cooler' compare two things. Warmer than what? Keep reading to find out!

quiz.question: How many seasons does Sam watch?
Why do new leaves grow in spring?
What happens to the leaves in autumn?
Why does the tree have no leaves in winter?

pages.text: Sam has a big tree outside the window and watches it change all year long. There are four {{seasons}}: spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

vocab.definition: The four parts of the year: spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

pages.text: In {{spring}}, the weather is mild. New leaves grow on the tree because the sun is {{warmer}}.

vocab.definition: The season after winter, when plants start to grow.
Having a higher temperature than before.

pages.text: In {{summer}}, the weather is hot. The tree has many green leaves because it gets a lot of sunlight.

vocab.definition: The hottest season of the year.

pages.text: In {{autumn}}, the weather is {{cooler}}. The leaves turn orange and fall to the ground.

vocab.definition: The season after summer, when leaves change color and fall.
Having a lower temperature than before.

pages.text: In {{winter}}, the weather is cold. The tree has no leaves because it is resting until spring.

vocab.definition: The coldest season of the year.

pages.text: The seasons are different in different parts of the {{world}}. What is the weather like where you live?

vocab.definition: The Earth, and everything and everyone on it.

title: Nora and the Water Cycle
summary: Have you ever wondered where rain comes from? Follow Nora as she discovers the water cycle.
teachingMethodReason: Meets Coyle, Hood & Marsh (2010)'s 4 C's Framework: Content - real earth-science knowledge (evaporation, condensation, precipitation as a repeating cycle), not just weather vocabulary; Communication - present-tense process description and "when/because" causal language are the vehicle for that content, with genuine technical terms (evaporation, condensation, precipitation) introduced because the content demands them; Cognition - the reader follows a cause-and-effect chain (heat -> vapor -> clouds -> rain -> repeat), a higher-order thinking skill beyond recall; Culture - the closing page (the cycle happens everywhere, from deserts to rainforests) is an intercultural/global-awareness note. Deliberately written in the simple present to describe a repeating process rather than the past-tense narrative this level's other books use (mystery-missing-cat, bens-missing-backpack), so the library covers a wider range of B1 grammar instead of repeating the same past-tense pattern.
grammarFeatures: Simple present tense for describing a repeating process
Sequencing connectors applied to a cycle (First, then, finally... and repeats)
introFunFacts: 🔁 A cycle goes round and round forever - so this story ends right back where it started!
🏷️ Watch for 'is called' - that's how we give something its proper science name.
🌡️ 'WHEN water gets hot...' - the word 'when' tells you the exact moment something changes.

quiz.question: What happens when the sun heats the water?
What is it called when vapor cools and becomes water drops?
Why does water fall back down from the clouds?
Does the water cycle ever stop?

options.label: No, it repeats again and again

pages.text: Nora loves rainy days. Have you ever wondered where rain comes from? It is all part of the {{water cycle}}.

vocab.definition: The way water moves between the sky and the ground, again and again.

pages.text: First, the sun heats the water in a lake or ocean. When water gets hot, it turns into an invisible gas called {{vapor}}. This is called {{evaporation}}.

vocab.definition: Water in the form of an invisible gas.
When water heats up and turns into vapor.

pages.text: The vapor rises into the sky. When it gets cold, it turns back into tiny drops of water. This is called {{condensation}}, and it forms {{clouds}}.

vocab.definition: When vapor cools down and turns back into water drops.
Groups of tiny water drops floating high in the sky.

pages.text: When the clouds get too heavy, the water falls back down as rain or snow. This is called {{precipitation}}.

vocab.definition: Rain, snow, or other water falling from clouds.

pages.text: The rain fills the rivers and oceans again. Because of this, the water cycle never stops - it repeats again and again!
The water cycle happens everywhere in the {{world}}, from deserts to rainforests. It gives every living thing the water it needs.

vocab.definition: The Earth, and everything and everyone on it.

title: Let's Move with Milo!
summary: Watch Milo, then you try! A read-aloud, act-it-out book of simple movement commands.
teachingMethodReason: The library's first genuine TPR book, built on Asher's actual structure from the course sources: comprehension-first, one real imperative command per page (Stand up!, Touch your toes!), Milo modeling the action, and no correction or production demanded from the reader - not a story that merely describes physical actions, which would just be Story-based. Honest limitation, stated plainly rather than glossed over: unlike a live TPR classroom, the app cannot see or verify whether the reader actually moves. It works as a command script for a reader (with a caregiver, realistically) to act out together, the same way a printed TPR flashcard set works - not a self-checking task like the library's TBL books, which is exactly why TPR and TBL have to stay separate categories rather than being reskins of each other.
grammarFeatures: Imperative mood (Stand up! Touch your toes!)
No tense marking - imperatives don't conjugate
